# Education in Finland
Finland’s education system includes a compulsory nine-year comprehensive school covering grades 1 to 9 (peruskoulu), expanded by legislation in 2021 to cover ages 7 to 18, including upper secondary school (lukio) or vocational school (ammattikoulu). The system avoids gifted programs, expecting advanced students to assist peers, and typically features small classes with fewer than twenty pupils. Schools emphasize multilingualism, arts, crafts, outdoor activities, minimal homework, and a relaxed atmosphere. Assessment initially may use verbal feedback, progressing to numerical grades on a 4–10 scale, with additional support provided instead of grade repetition whenever possible. Education and social support, including free school health care, meals, materials, and travel, are provided to students.
Upper secondary education (ages 15–18) has become compulsory as of 2021, offering academic (lukio) and vocational tracks with flexible pathways and the possibility for vocational graduates to enter higher education. Admissions to academic upper schools depend on GPA and exams, culminating in a prestigious matriculation examination, which remains a key university admission criterion. Teachers must hold master's degrees, and teaching is a highly respected profession with competitive university entry. Tertiary education is divided into traditional research universities focusing on theoretical education and universities of applied sciences emphasizing practical skills and industry collaboration. Selection is merit-based, transparent, and relies on final grades and entrance exams without subjective factors like essays or extracurriculars. Tuition has been free for EU students until 2017, when fees were introduced for non-EEA students. Adult education includes diverse “Free Education” institutes offering non-degree courses for personal development, and Open University programs allow non-student adults to enroll in individual university courses.
Finland actively promotes foreign language proficiency, requires at least two additional languages besides the mother tongue, and supports educational export models abroad. Recent reforms, including the 2016 National Curriculum Framework, incorporate phenomenon-based learning alongside traditional subjects to foster 21st-century skills such as collaboration, critical thinking, creativity, and communication.
